nodes.title: Solomon Secured; Wisdom Granted
nodes.summary: Amid deathbed intrigue David names Solomon king, and the young ruler asks God not for wealth or long life but for a discerning heart — receiving wisdom that draws the world to his court. The famous split-the-baby judgment shows it in action.

prerequisites.reason: The succession struggle continues 2 Samuel's court narrative; David's charge to Solomon assumes his whole reign.
Solomon is the first test of the dynastic promise — the 'son' language of the covenant hangs over his whole reign.

connections.reason: Proverbs presents itself as the deposit of the Solomonic wisdom granted here.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Offered anything he wanted, Solomon asks for a discerning heart to govern God's people. What does his request reveal about what wisdom is actually for, and if God asked you the same question tonight, what would your honest answer be?
assessment_questions: What does Solomon ask God for at Gibeon, and what does God give him beyond his request?
In the dispute between the two mothers, Solomon has no witnesses and no evidence. How does his ruling show what a discerning heart looks like in practice?
Solomon asked for wisdom to serve people rather than for things that would serve himself. What decision are you facing where asking for discernment first would change what you do?

teaching_concepts.concept: God keeps the Davidic promise through messy politics
teaching_concepts.explanation: Solomon reaches the throne amid intrigue and rivalry, yet God's covenant with David moves forward exactly as promised.

teaching_concepts.concept: Wisdom is a gift to ask for
teaching_concepts.explanation: Solomon receives discernment because he asks God for it in humility, and the story treats that request as the best prayer he ever prayed.
The judgment between the two mothers shows that real wisdom defends the vulnerable instead of impressing an audience.
God ties continued blessing to obedience in David's charge, since even a God-given gift like wisdom needs a heart that stays true.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what Solomon asked for at Gibeon and how the judgment between the two mothers shows that wisdom in action.

comprehension_check.question: 1 Kings 1 is all palace intrigue: rival feasts, hurried alliances, a rushed anointing. What is the chapter showing about God's promise to David?
options: Only Nathan's quick maneuvering saved a promise that had failed
The promise passes to whichever son proves the boldest claimant
The promise moves forward even through court scheming and rivalry
The promise was suspended until Solomon could earn the throne
comprehension_check.why: Solomon is crowned because David keeps an oath sworn by the LORD in 1 Kings 1:29-30, so the succession lands where the promise pointed.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 1:29-30. Notice what David appeals to when he finally settles who will reign.

comprehension_check.question: All Israel hears the verdict between the two mothers and stands in awe (1 Kings 3:28). What has the judgment shown them?
options: God's gift of wisdom in their king works to do justice
Their king can outwit any liar who enters his court
A ruler may bend the truth whenever a case demands it
Fear of the throne will now keep order in Israel
comprehension_check.why: 1 Kings 3:28 says the awe came from seeing God-given wisdom applied to justice, the gift Solomon had asked for in 1 Kings 3:9.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 3:9 and 1 Kings 3:28 together. Notice what Solomon asks the gift for, and what Israel concludes from the verdict.

nodes.title: The Temple
nodes.summary: Solomon builds the temple, the ark enters, and the glory-cloud that once filled the tabernacle fills the house — while Solomon's dedication prayer already anticipates exile and pleads that God hear the penitent 'toward this place.' The tabernacle's portable Eden becomes stone and gold on Zion.

prerequisites.reason: The temple is the tabernacle made permanent; the descending glory deliberately repeats Exodus 40.
The building project is the centerpiece of Solomon's reign as established in chapters 1-4.

connections.reason: 'The Word became flesh and dwelt among us' presents Jesus as the true temple — glory in a human body.
Chronicles retells the temple construction with its own post-exilic emphasis.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Solomon builds God a magnificent house and then prays that even the highest heaven cannot contain him. How can both be true at once, and what difference does it make to know that the God you pray to is both near and beyond every place built for him?
assessment_questions: What fills the temple when the priests bring the ark into the inner sanctuary, and how do the priests respond?
Solomon says heaven itself cannot contain God, yet he asks God to hear every prayer made toward this house. What does his prayer teach about how God chooses to meet his people?
Solomon's dedication prayer keeps returning to forgiveness for people who sin and then turn back. What would it look like for your own prayers to lean that confidently on God's readiness to forgive?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The temple completes what God promised David, showing that God's commitments hold across generations and delays.

teaching_concepts.concept: The temple as the place of God's presence
teaching_concepts.explanation: The glory-cloud filling the house marks the temple as the place where God chooses to dwell among his people.
Solomon confesses that no building can hold the Creator, so the temple points beyond itself to a God greater than any sign of him.
Solomon's prayer models worship that mixes praise with honest confession and counts on God's mercy when people fail.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe what happens when the ark enters the temple, and explain how Solomon's prayer holds together God's presence in the house and God's greatness beyond it.

comprehension_check.question: In his dedication prayer Solomon says even the highest heavens cannot contain God (1 Kings 8:27). What does that make of the temple he just built?
options: The one place on earth where God may now be found
A meeting place God chose that points beyond itself to him
A house whose rituals guarantee the nation's lasting security
A tribute whose splendor earns God's attention to its prayers
comprehension_check.why: In 1 Kings 8:29-30 Solomon asks the God who dwells in heaven to keep his Name and his ear turned toward this house.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 8:27-30. Notice where Solomon says God dwells, and what he asks the building to be for.

comprehension_check.question: Solomon's long dedication prayer keeps imagining failure: defeat, drought, famine, even exile (1 Kings 8:33-50). Why fill a dedication with disasters?
options: Solomon privately doubts the value of the house he built
Listing the dangers wards them off before they can arrive
The disasters threaten only nations that have no temple
The temple is where penitent failures turn to find forgiveness
comprehension_check.why: 1 Kings 8:30 sets the pattern of the whole prayer, heaven's ear open toward this place whenever failed people turn back to plead.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 8:46-50. Notice what Solomon asks God to do when the people have sinned and been carried far away.

nodes.title: The Glory and Fall of Solomon
nodes.summary: The queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon and leaves breathless — then the same king amasses horses, gold, and seven hundred wives, and his heart turns to other gods. The wisest man in the world breaks every rule in Deuteronomy's law of the king, and God tears the kingdom in two.

prerequisites.reason: The fall's tragedy is measured against the temple builder's height.
1 Kgs 9–11 judges Solomon by the royal limits set in Deut 17 (no many horses, wives, or gold), a legal standard the narrative presumes but does not restate.

connections.reason: Jesus invokes this scene: 'the queen of the South came to hear Solomon — and something greater than Solomon is here.'

nodes.discussion_prompt: The wisest man alive drifts into worshiping other gods, one marriage and one alliance at a time. What do these chapters show about how a heart turns, and what small compromise in your own life would look exactly like this if it kept growing?
assessment_questions: What draws the queen of Sheba to Jerusalem, and what does she conclude after seeing Solomon's court?
The narrator says Solomon's heart was not fully devoted to the LORD in his old age. Why does the story locate his fall in his heart rather than in his circumstances?
Solomon's gifts and success did not protect his devotion. Where in your life could success itself become the thing that pulls you away from God, and what guard would you put in place?

teaching_concepts.explanation: God renews his promise to Solomon while tying continued favor to obedience, so privilege never cancels responsibility.

teaching_concepts.concept: Success is no shield for the heart
teaching_concepts.explanation: Solomon's fame and wealth coexist with a slow turn away from God, proving that gifts and devotion are two different things.
Solomon's accumulating wives and alliances pull his worship after their gods, showing how small accommodations grow into open unfaithfulness.
God tears the kingdom in judgment yet preserves David's line and one tribe, holding justice and promise together.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how Solomon's reign moves from the queen of Sheba's praise to God's announcement of judgment, and name what turned his heart.

comprehension_check.question: The king who received wisdom straight from God ends 1 Kings 11 building shrines for other gods. What does his fall teach about God's gifts?
options: A gift never substitutes for a heart kept devoted
The wisdom God gave must have faded as Solomon aged
His celebrated wisdom had been courtly legend, never God's gift
Wealth that great proves God's favor never left him
comprehension_check.why: 1 Kings 11:4 locates the collapse in an aging king's divided heart, while 1 Kings 9:4 had conditioned blessing on integrity before God.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 9:4-5 and 1 Kings 11:4. Notice the condition God states, and what the narrator says eventually happened inside Solomon.

comprehension_check.question: God's sentence on Solomon tears the kingdom away yet leaves one tribe and a lamp for David (1 Kings 11:11-13, 11:36). What is the sentence doing?
options: Reducing the loss to a warning that never takes effect
Proving the covenant with David has now been revoked
Holding real judgment and the promise to David together
Letting politics run its course without any divine involvement
comprehension_check.why: 1 Kings 11:36 preserves David's line and city even while the kingdom is torn, covenant faithfulness working inside real judgment.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 11:11-13. Notice what God says he will take, what he will keep, and for whose sake.

nodes.title: The Kingdom Divided
nodes.summary: Rehoboam's arrogance splits the nation: ten tribes follow Jeroboam north (Israel), two stay with David's line in Jerusalem (Judah). Jeroboam's golden calves at Bethel and Dan institutionalize idolatry, and king after king 'walked in his sin' — the drumbeat of both books of Kings.

prerequisites.reason: The split is the judgment announced on Solomon's apostasy; Jeroboam was promised the ten tribes in chapter 11.

1 Kgs 12–16 assumes the reader will recognize Jeroboam's "your gods who brought you out of Egypt" and calf-worship as a replay of Exodus 32's covenant-breach, a theological echo the narrative does not re-explain.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Jeroboam builds golden calves because sending worshipers to Jerusalem feels politically risky. When has convenience quietly reshaped what worship or obedience looks like in your world, and how would you recognize it happening?
assessment_questions: Why do the ten northern tribes break away from Rehoboam, and who becomes their first king?

Jeroboam sets up calves at Bethel and Dan and says these gods brought Israel out of Egypt. Why does the story treat his practical religious solution as the sin that defines every northern king after him?
Rehoboam rejects the elders' counsel for the advice of his young friends. Whose counsel do you actually weigh when you make decisions, and what would taking wise counsel seriously change?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Rehoboam's refusal to listen to wise counsel costs him ten tribes, showing how arrogant leadership brings communal disaster.
Jeroboam's calves look like practical religion, and the story exposes them as apostasy that cuts a nation off from God.
Prophets keep interrupting royal plans in these chapters, and ignoring their warnings consistently invites judgment.
God keeps his commitment to David's line while still judging each king by covenant faithfulness, so mercy never erases responsibility.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell how the kingdom split under Rehoboam, and explain why Jeroboam's golden calves become the measuring stick for every northern king.

comprehension_check.question: At the moment Rehoboam refuses to listen, the narrator points behind the scene to the LORD's own word (1 Kings 12:15). What is that note claiming?
options: Rehoboam bears no blame since the outcome was fixed
God abandoned the whole nation to its political fate
The kingdom fell to chance the narrator dresses in piety
The split executes the judgment God had already announced
comprehension_check.why: 1 Kings 12:15 ties the disaster to the word spoken through Ahijah, the judgment announced in 1 Kings 11:11 now arriving on schedule.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 11:11 and then 1 Kings 12:15. Notice whose earlier sentence the narrator says this moment fulfills.

comprehension_check.question: Jeroboam sets up the golden calves only after some anxious arithmetic in his heart (1 Kings 12:26-28). What does the story expose in his new religion?
options: A sincere reform God accepted although its style was irregular
Worship engineered to protect a throne, whatever God had commanded
A forgivable compromise that later kings quietly walked back
An honest guess at worship by a king without guidance
comprehension_check.why: 1 Kings 12:26-27 shows the calves born of political fear about pilgrims returning to Jerusalem, and 1 Kings 13:34 names the result sin.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 12:26-28. Notice what Jeroboam is worried about before he ever says a word about worship.

nodes.title: Elijah vs. Baal
nodes.summary: Against Ahab and Jezebel's state-sponsored Baal cult, Elijah shuts the sky, calls down fire on Mount Carmel, then collapses into despair and meets God not in wind or earthquake but a low whisper. Naboth's stolen vineyard shows what the fight is about: kings who devour their own people.

prerequisites.reason: Elijah's ministry targets the Omride dynasty and Baal establishment those chapters build.

connections.reason: Elijah stands with Moses at the Transfiguration — the prophets personified beside the law.
James holds up Elijah's prayer that shut the sky as the model of effective righteous prayer.
Paul cites God's 'seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal' as the pattern of the faithful remnant.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Elijah asks the people how long they will waver between two opinions. Where in these chapters does God prove himself with fire, where does he speak in a whisper, and what would it mean for you to stop wavering between two loyalties this week?
assessment_questions: What happens on Mount Carmel when Elijah and the prophets of Baal each prepare a sacrifice?

Right after the fire falls at Carmel, Elijah collapses into despair, and God passes by in a low whisper rather than in wind, earthquake, or fire. What does that scene teach about how God meets a discouraged servant?
Naboth dies so a king can have a vegetable garden, and God sends Elijah to name the crime. What injustice near you needs someone willing to speak, and what holds you back?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Elijah is fed by ravens and a starving widow, showing that God sustains his servants in surprising ways when he calls them into conflict.
Carmel puts Baal to a public test and fire answers only the LORD, so worship is a real decision between rival claims rather than a mood.
At Horeb God meets Elijah's despair with food, rest, a whisper, and a new assignment, treating exhaustion with care instead of rebuke.
Naboth's vineyard shows God taking the side of the powerless, since no crown puts a person above the covenant.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the contest on Mount Carmel and explain what Elijah's encounter with God at Horeb adds to the picture of who God is.

comprehension_check.question: On Carmel, Elijah gives Baal's prophets every advantage and all day (1 Kings 18:21-39). What is the contest built to settle?
options: Whether the LORD or Baal is God, ending Israel's hedging
Whether prayer works better when it is loud and desperate
Whether Baal deserves a lesser place under the LORD
Whether Israel's drought came from angering the storm god
comprehension_check.why: 1 Kings 18:24 makes an answered altar the deciding test between rival gods, and 1 Kings 18:39 records Israel's verdict.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 18:21. Notice the question Elijah puts to the people before any altar is built.

comprehension_check.question: After Carmel's triumph, Elijah flees to Horeb asking to die (1 Kings 19:4). How does God handle his collapsed prophet?
options: With a public rebuke that shames him into returning
With agreement that Israel's apostasy is now past remedy
With food, rest, his own presence, and further work
With silence until the prophet's despair burns itself out
comprehension_check.why: The angel feeds him twice in 1 Kings 19:5-7, and in 1 Kings 19:15-16 God entrusts him with new assignments.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 19:5-8 and 1 Kings 19:15-18. Notice what God provides before asking anything, and what work still waits.
